description: Hey, I’m Dhyanesh, Grade 11 IB student in Toronto. I’ve coded in Python and Java since Grade 5 and like building things that react in real life. My last hackathon team won Best Use of Open Source AI with CaptainGemma. Now we’re building a spacecraft orbit sim that avoids debris and asteroids, plus a controller and a small sensor robot. Looking for: electronics, CAD/3D printing, UI design, presenting, physics/math. Portfolio: https://dhyaneshdev.vercel.app/
summary: T-Minus_6, developed by Team D NOVAS, is an interactive STEM project that combines a physical four-wheel robotic rover with a digital spacecraft simulation to introduce students to the challenges of operating in space. The project features two complementary demonstrations: a physical robotic platform showcasing electronic systems and hazard visualization, and a 2D orbital spacecraft simulation featuring Earth, orbital movement, and environmental hazards. The simulation includes orbital debris, asteroid events, extreme temperature conditions, and a mission-life system that demonstrates the consequences of collisions. The physical rover incorporates electronic components, motor control, and a breadboard circuit, while an updated asteroid tower uses a green laser to indicate a simulated impact location. By combining robotics, programming, electronics, and interactive simulation, T-Minus_6 provides a hands-on learning experience designed to introduce students aged 7–12 to aerospace engineering and inspire further exploration of STEM.
details:
Project Functionality and Technical Operation

T-Minus_6 is a physical and digital STEM project designed to demonstrate different engineering challenges associated with spacecraft operation and safety. It consists of two complementary components: a physical four-wheel robotic rover and a digital 2D orbital spacecraft simulation.

The digital simulation recreates an orbital environment featuring Earth, an orbital path, and different environmental hazards. Players navigate a virtual spacecraft while encountering orbital debris, simulated asteroid events, and extreme temperature conditions. The simulation incorporates a mission-life system that begins with 15 lives. Collisions reduce the remaining lives, and reaching zero triggers a mission-failure sequence.

The physical component is a four-wheel robotic platform that demonstrates robotics, electronic systems, and motor control. Its hardware architecture incorporates Arduino microcontrollers, a motor driver, sensors, and electronic components. The updated asteroid tower uses a green laser pointer to indicate the ground location corresponding to a simulated asteroid impact. A breadboard-based circuit is also used to demonstrate different electronic operating cases.

The physical rover and digital simulation are separate demonstrations rather than synchronized systems. Together, they introduce students to different aspects of spacecraft engineering, hazard awareness, and interactive simulation.

Hardware and Software

The project uses a combination of embedded electronics, robotics components, and software development tools.

Documented hardware components include Arduino UNO Q and Arduino UNO R3 boards, a TB6612FNG motor driver, TT gear motors, an HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor, a DHT11 temperature and humidity sensor, breadboards, LCD displays, LEDs, buzzers, and supporting electronic components. The physical platform uses a four-wheel configuration, with an updated green laser indicator for visualizing simulated asteroid impact locations.

The digital simulation is developed using Python 3 and Pygame for its graphical interface and gameplay mechanics. PySerial is used for serial communication functionality. Arduino IDE supports embedded development, while VS Code and GitHub are used for programming and project management.

Some planned functionalities, including autonomous navigation and temperature-warning operation, were not fully operational in the final prototype. These remain areas for future development.

Creativity and Innovation

The primary creative aspect of T-Minus_6 is its combination of a physical robotic platform and a digital spacecraft simulation to introduce different aspects of spaceflight engineering.

The physical rover provides a practical demonstration of robotics and electronic systems, while the orbital simulation allows students to explore spacecraft navigation and environmental hazards in a controlled digital environment.

The updated asteroid tower introduces a physical visual representation of a simulated hazard through a green laser impact-location indicator. The breadboard circuit also provides an opportunity to demonstrate different electronic operating cases.

By combining hardware construction, software development, and interactive learning, the project explores multiple approaches to making aerospace engineering more accessible.

Educational Benefits and Intended Impact

T-Minus_6 is primarily intended for students aged 7–12. Its objective is to introduce younger learners to aerospace engineering and the challenges associated with spacecraft operation through practical and interactive demonstrations.

The project introduces concepts such as orbital hazards, collision risks, environmental monitoring, robotics, motor control, sensors, and embedded programming. Students can explore the digital simulation to understand the consequences of spacecraft hazards while observing the physical rover and its electronic systems to gain exposure to real engineering components.

The project has potential applications in classroom STEM activities, robotics workshops, and interactive science education programs.

Ultimately, T-Minus_6 aims to encourage curiosity about aerospace engineering, robotics, computer science, and future space exploration by making complex engineering concepts more accessible to younger students.
